name: D-aspartic acid (DAA)

card.summary: An amino acid sold as a testosterone booster; early work suggested a hormonal role, but trials in trained men found no increase and, at higher intake, a decrease.
card.note: Three randomized trials in resistance-trained men reported no testosterone increase; one reported lower testosterone at the higher intake tested.

quick.overview:
D-aspartic acid is the mirror-image (D-form) of the common amino acid aspartic acid, found naturally in the pituitary gland and testes. It is sold as a sports supplement marketed for raising testosterone.

A 2009 study reported that sodium D-aspartate increased luteinizing hormone and testosterone in humans and rats. Later randomized trials in resistance-trained men found no testosterone rise, and one found lower testosterone at 6 grams per day.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory work in rats proposes that D-aspartate acts in the pituitary to increase LH release and in testicular Leydig cells to raise testosterone synthesis, via cGMP and cAMP signaling. Human trials in trained men did not show this effect.
quick.risks: The trials report no major safety signals, but one reported lower total and free testosterone with 6 g/day, and another reported a 16 percent drop in estradiol. It is sold as a dietary supplement; long-term safety data are limited.

lead: D-aspartic acid (DAA) is the D-enantiomer of aspartic acid, one of two D-amino acids commonly found in mammals; it is largely not used to build proteins and is found in tissues including the pituitary gland and testes [1][3]. It is sold as a dietary supplement marketed for raising testosterone, particularly to men who lift weights.

The marketing rests on a 2009 report that sodium D-aspartate raised luteinizing hormone (LH) and testosterone in humans and rats [3]. Subsequent randomized, placebo-controlled trials in resistance-trained men published between 2013 and 2017 found no increase in testosterone, and one found lower testosterone at the higher intake tested [4].

paras: The 2009 study reported that the pituitary and testes synthesize D-aspartate from L-aspartate and take it up efficiently. In rat pituitary tissue it increased LH release and synthesis via cGMP signaling, and in rat Leydig cells it increased testosterone synthesis and release via cAMP [3]. Aspartate-related compounds such as NMDA act on glutamate receptors in the nervous system; D-aspartate is also described as a neuromodulator [1].
The 2009 report included a human component in which sodium D-aspartate was associated with higher LH and testosterone [3].

In a 2013 trial in resistance-trained men, 28 days of DAA with heavy training did not change total or free testosterone, LH, GnRH or estradiol, and body composition and strength improved equally in both groups; the authors concluded it had no anabolic or ergogenic effect at the dose given [4]. A 2015 trial compared 3 g and 6 g daily in trained men: 3 g did not differ from placebo, while 6 g was associated with lower total and free testosterone [4]. A 2017 randomized trial over three months found no change in basal total or free testosterone, a 16 percent fall in estradiol, and similar strength and muscle-size gains in DAA and placebo groups; its authors wrote that DAA is ineffective at changing testosterone levels [4].
Published trials have mostly enrolled young, resistance-trained men; studies in men with low testosterone or infertility are less documented in the sources reviewed here.

The trials above did not report serious adverse events, but did report changes in hormone levels: lower total and free testosterone with 6 g/day in one trial, and reduced estradiol in another [4]. No long-term safety studies are available.
DAA is sold in the US as a dietary supplement, often in pre-workout and testosterone-support blends. The sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing-forum discussion of the compound.

timeline.event: Report that sodium D-aspartate raised LH and testosterone in humans and rats [3]
Placebo-controlled trial in trained men finds no hormonal or performance effect [4]
Trial finds 3 g no different from placebo and 6 g associated with lower testosterone [4]
Three-month trial finds no testosterone change [4]
